speaker: Doctor
text: Welcome to the clinic. I understand you are here because of a neck swelling; to help me determine the cause, please describe exactly where the lump is located, how long it has been there, and if it changes size or is painful to the touch.

speaker: Patient
text: 50-year-old male. The patient reports a progressively increasing swelling on the nape of his neck for 2 months. He denies having a fever, pain, or any discharge from the swelling. He mentions a history of colon cancer for which he underwent colectomy at the age of 43. He also has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and osteoarthritis of the left knee. He takes insulin glargine, metformin, enalapril, and naproxen.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Metastatic Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Neck (Cervical Lymphadenopathy) secondary to Head and Neck Primary (likely occult) or Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Esophagus.

I have noted your history of colon cancer, but the location of this new swelling at the nape of the neck, combined with your age and lack of systemic symptoms like fever, strongly suggests a metastatic process from a head and neck primary tumor rather than a recurrence of your previous colon cancer. Given your history of diabetes and hypertension, we must also rule out infectious causes, though the chronicity makes infection less likely. To confirm the nature of this mass, I need to see imaging and potentially a biopsy. REQUEST IMAGES: Neck Ultrasound and CT Neck/Chest/Abdomen/Pelvis. REQUEST TEST: Fine Needle Aspiration (FNA) of the cervical lymph node.
